full_judgment:
4. The trial Court disallowed the case for pre-emption on the only observation that the petitioner is a co-sharer by purchase and the purchaser O.Ps. are co-sharer by inheritance and as such this case for pre-emption is not maintainable as per clause A of section 96(10) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Against this judgment and order of the trial court the petitioner preferred the above mentioned miscellaneous appeal and the learned appellate court also disallowed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and order of the learned trial court making further observation that this case for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties for non-impleading a daughter of original owner Garibullah. The learned appellate court, in his impugned judgment has confirmed the view of the learned trial court to the effect that this case for pre-emption is not maintainable as it has been filed by a co-sharer by purchase in respect of a sale in favour of co-sharer by inheritance. 

 7. I have heard the learned lawyers for both the parties at length and examined the lower court's record minutely. It appears that in the very petition for pre-emption petitioner has categorically stated that he is a co-sharer of the holding of the schedule I land and he prays for pre-emption of schedule 1 land only. Admittedly the O.P. purchasers are not co-sharers of the holding of schedule 1 land. Before this court also the learned lawyers for purchaser opposite parties has admitted that the petitioner is a co-sharer of holding of schedule 1 by virtue of purchase and the purchasers opposite-parties Nos. 1-4 stranger to that. There is no denial of the fact that the petitioner has filed this case for pre-emption within the statutory period of limitation and he is also otherwise entitled to get pre-emption of the land of schedule-1. But it appears that both the courts below have committed grave error holding that the purchaser opposite parties 1-4 are the co-sharers of the holding of schedule-1 also by virtue of inheritance and as such the petitioner, being a co-sharer by purchase, cannot get the pre-emption of the land of schedule-1. 

 8. However, in this revisional application the only point which has been agitated by the parties is whether this case for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties or not admittedly one Goribullah was the original owner of the land of schedule. 1 and this Goribullah died leaving son the vendor opposite party No. 5. In the written objection the opposite party Nos. 1-4 have stated only that after the death of Goribullah, the opposite party No. 5 inherited the schedule-1 land. In this written objection though there is a general denial that the case is bad for defect of parties but there is not a single word to the effect that Garibullah left any daughter also. After commencement of the trial, for the first time, the purchaser opposite parties made an allegation that Goribullah died leaving a daughter also namely Nadirunnessa and that as this Nadirunnessa had not been impleaded as a party this case for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties. However the trial court did not frame any issue as to whether the case is bad for defect of parties and did not make any findings as to defect of parties. But the learned appellate court in his impugned judgment has made an observation that Goribullah died leaving a daughter also namely Nadirunnessa and this case for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties for not impleading this Nadirunnessa as a party. The learned lawyer for the petitioner has made submission before this to the effect that this question as to defect of parties has not been raised by the opposite party purchasers at the early stage of the case and only after the commencement of the trial of the case the opposite party purchasers made a story that Goribullah had a daughter named Nadirunnessa. The learned Counsel's contention is that this belated objection as to the defect of parties has not been proved also and as such the learned appellate court has made an error of law holding the case for a pre-emption as bad for defect of parties. 

 9. In reply the learned counsel for, the purchaser opposite parties has made submission to the effect that in the trial court the petitioner himself has admitted during cross-examination that Goribullah had a daughter named Nadirunnessa. But the learned lawyer for the petitioner has submitted that infect the petitioner denied the suggestion of the learned Counsel of the opposite party to the effect that Garibullah had a daughter named Nadirunnessa but inadvertently the reply of the petitioner was written down in affirmative. That in fact the P.W.1 did never admit that Goribullah had a daughter Nadirunnessa by name. To substantiate his contention the .learned lawyer has pointed out that immediate after recording of this evidence of the P.W.1 on 19.7.80 the petitioner filed a verified petition on 22.7.80 stating that he never admitted that Goribullah had a daughter and that inadvertently it had been written so in his cross-examination. However, I have examined the L.C. Record. It appears that the learned trial court considered this petition of the petitioner submitted on 22.7.80 but did not pass any order either allowing or rejecting the petition. The learned court simply made an order that the said petition be kept with the record. However, it cannot be denied that after submission of that petition by the petitioner the fact stood that the petitioner did not admit that Goribullah had a daughter, Nadirunnessa by name. So in this circumstances where there is no specific assertion in the pleading of the purchaser opposite parties to the effect that Goribullah had a daughter the onus was entirely upon this opposite parties to prove that actually Goribullah had a daughter namely Nadirunnessa. But it appears that the purchasers opposite parties could not bring a single iota of evidence before the court to prove that Goribullah had a daughter named Nadirunnessa. So in this circumstances I am of opinion that where the purchaser opposite parties failed to raise the objection as to defect of parties at the earliest stage of the case and where at the trial also they could not bring any evidence to prove this objection as to defect of parties in spite of the fact that long before commencement of the evidence of the contesting opposite parties side the petitioner filed an verified petition on 22.7.80 denying the existence of any daughter of Goribullah the learned appellate Court has made an error of both law and fact holding this case for pre-emption as bad for defect of parties and this error has occasioned a failure of justice. In a recent case reported in 49 DLR(AD) at page 151 it has been held by their lordships that no suit can fail by reason merely of non joinder of parties. However, considering the facts and circumstances stated above I am of opinion that the learned appellate court has acted illegally in dismissing the case for pre-emption on ground for defect of parties.
